content: A nipple is a structure from which fluid is released. In mammals, it is the projection on the breast that delivers milk to the offspring. In mammalian anatomy, the nipple, also known as the mammary papilla, is a small projection of skin that contains the outlets for 15 to 20 lactiferous ducts, which are arranged in a cylindrical pattern around the tip. The skin of the nipple is highly innervated with specialized nerves that are sensitive to specific stimuli. The primary physiological function of nipples is to deliver milk to infants, which is produced in the female mammary glands during lactation. In males, nipples are generally not functional for breastfeeding, although male lactation is possible. Mammalian infants exhibit a rooting instinct to locate the nipple and a sucking instinct to extract milk. Mammals typically have an even number of nipples arranged bilaterally. These develop during embryogenesis along the milk lines, with the number of nipples on one side often correlating with the average litter size of the species. In primitive mammals, such as monotremes like the platypus, the mammary glands release milk directly onto the skin without the presence of a nipple. Most humans are born with two nipples, located near the center of each breast and surrounded by a pigmented, sensitive area of skin called the areola. During fetal development, humans initially form multiple nipples along the milk lines, which extend from the armpit to the groin on both sides. These additional nipples usually regress before birth, but in some cases, they persist, resulting in supernumerary nipples, which may occasionally have functional lactiferous glands. The pigmentation of the nipple and areola is due to brown eumelanin and, to a greater extent, red pheomelanin. In both males and females, the nipple and areola can serve as erogenous zones or be considered secondary sexual organs. Stimulation or sexual arousal can cause the nipples to become erect, a response mediated by the release of the neuropeptide oxytocin. This effect can also occur during breastfeeding or exposure to cold temperatures. Pregnancy and nursing often lead to an increase in nipple size, which may sometimes be permanent, as well as an increase in pigmentation. The erection of the nipple is partially due to the presence of cylindrical muscle cells within the structure. In many women, small protrusions on the areola, known as Montgomery glands, are present. Occasionally, newborns, regardless of sex, may produce milk, a phenomenon referred to as witch's milk. This is caused by maternal estrogens acting on the baby and is considered normal. The production of witch's milk typically resolves within a few days. In male mammals, nipples form during early fetal development. Up until approximately 14 weeks of gestation, all mammalian fetuses of the same species appear identical, regardless of sex. After this point, genetically male fetuses begin producing male hormones, such as testosterone. Since the default developmental pathway in mammals is female, nipples have already formed by the time male differentiation begins. Studies have shown that female nipples are erect during the fetal stage in mammals, along with other forms of arousal. In most cases, male nipples do not undergo significant changes after this stage. However, some males may develop a condition called gynecomastia, in which the fatty tissue around and beneath the nipple enlarges, resembling a female breast. In males who develop gynecomastia during puberty, the condition is often temporary unless they are obese. Gynecomastia can also occur when testosterone levels drop, such as due to certain medications.
